title: A helper inside your workshop

beats.say: What is the difference between asking a stranger for advice, and hiring a helper who walks into your workshop?

Pasting code into a chat is like describing your kitchen over the phone. The advice is a guess. Claude Code is the helper standing in the kitchen. It opens your files, searches them, and runs your tests, so it answers from what is really there.
But a helper in your kitchen can also break things. So it asks before anything risky, like running a command. You stay the boss, and you can say stop any time by pressing Escape.
One catch. Each visit starts with a blank memory. Anything it should always know goes on a note on the fridge: a file in your project called CLAUDE dot M D.

check.q: What main advantage does Claude Code have over pasting code into a chat window?
opts: It can see and run your real project
It never makes mistakes
It remembers every past session
It works without any approvals
check.why: It opens real files, searches and runs tests, so answers are grounded in your code rather than a guess. It can still be wrong, asks for approval on risky steps, and forgets between sessions.

work: Pick one small bug in your repo and describe it to Claude Code in a single plain sentence.
Write down three facts about your project a newcomer would need, as a first draft of a CLAUDE.md note.

title: The loop behind every task

beats.say: What actually happens between you typing one sentence and Claude changing your code?

You type a task, like: why does this dbt model double count. Claude does not just answer. It calls tools. It reads the model file, searches the repo for the join, and runs the tests. Each result comes back to it as new information.
That is the loop. Think, use a tool, read the result, repeat. One task may take ten or twenty tool calls. Risky ones, like editing a file or running a shell command, pause and wait for your approval.
The loop ends when Claude gives you an answer, or when you press Escape. Then you review the changes, because the edits are real.

check.q: Why does Claude Code call several tools before giving an answer?
opts: To slow itself down on purpose
Each tool result gives it facts to decide the next step
Because chat models cannot produce text alone
Because you must approve every answer
check.why: It works in a loop: each tool result, such as a file read or a test run, becomes new information that guides the next step until the task is done.

work: Watch one session and count how many tool calls it makes before answering.
Read each approval prompt fully before you accept it, for one whole day.

title: Where the gotchas hide

beats.say: Why did Claude forget everything you told it yesterday?

Because every session starts empty. Only files on disk carry over. Rules like use our naming convention, or never run against production, must live in CLAUDE dot M D in the repo, which it reads at the start.
Second gotcha: it acts. A backfill run against the wrong warehouse is a real incident. Approval prompts are your guardrail, but if you click yes without reading, the guardrail is gone.
Third: it only knows what it has opened. A long session fills its working memory, and early details blur. Start fresh for each new task, and run the tests yourself.

check.q: A rule such as never run against production keeps being ignored in new sessions. What is the best fix?
opts: Repeat it louder in every chat
Put it in CLAUDE.md in the repo
Hope the model remembers
Use one very long session
check.why: Sessions start fresh, so durable rules must be in a file the agent reads at the start. Long sessions also blur early details, so they are not a fix.

work: Add a short never-do list, such as no production writes, to your repo's CLAUDE.md.
Start a new session for each unrelated task instead of reusing one long chat.

title: When not to reach for the agent

beats.say: When is an agent in your terminal the wrong tool?

When the job is mechanical and repeatable, like renaming a column across two hundred models. A scripted codemod is cheaper, gives the same result every run, and is easy to test. An agent costs tokens at every step, and can vary.
Use the agent where the work is fuzzy: debugging, exploring unfamiliar code, drafting tests. Give it read-only warehouse credentials and a dev schema, so its worst mistake is cheap.
The real limit is not typing speed. It is review. If it writes in minutes what takes you an hour to check, you gain nothing. Keep tasks small, so each change can be reviewed in minutes.

check.q: You must rename one column in 200 dbt models in an identical way. What is the best choice?
opts: Ask the agent to edit each file by hand
A scripted codemod, reviewed once
Skip tests because the change is simple
Give the agent production write access
check.why: Mechanical, repeatable edits suit a deterministic script: cheaper, identical every run, easy to test. Save the agent for fuzzy work, and keep review effort in mind.

work: List your team's repeated mechanical changes and write scripts for them, not agent prompts.
Set up a dev schema and read-only credentials for agent sessions.

title: Install and sign in, the everyday version

beats.say: What does it take to bring a helper into your computer? Two things: let it in, and prove who is paying.

Installing is like moving a new tool into your toolbox. You paste one line into the Terminal, the text window where you type commands to your Mac. That line fetches Claude Code and puts it where your Mac can find it.
Signing in is like showing a membership card at the gym door. The first time you start it, it asks who is paying: your Claude subscription, or a developer account that charges for each use.

check.q: In the analogy, what does signing in correspond to?
opts: Moving the tool into the toolbox
Showing a membership card to prove who is paying
Opening the Terminal window
check.why: Installing puts the tool on your Mac. Signing in proves which account is paying for your use.

work: Open Terminal on your Mac and find out which of the two install lines you will use.
Decide before you start whether you will sign in with a subscription or a Console account.

title: What the install line and first run really do

beats.say: What actually happens when you paste that install line?

Curl downloads a small script from claude dot ai. Bash runs it. The script fetches the Claude Code program and drops it in a folder your terminal searches for commands, so typing claude works from anywhere.
Now go into a project folder and type claude. It treats that folder as its workspace, so it only works on the files you chose. The first run opens a browser to sign in.
Pick a Pro or Max subscription for a flat monthly price, or a Console account billed per token, a token being a small chunk of text. Then run slash doctor to check the setup.

show.title: Two ways to sign in
items: Pro or Max: flat monthly price

check.q: Why can you type claude from any folder after the install?
opts: The script placed the program in a folder the terminal searches for commands
Curl runs every time you type claude
Your browser keeps a copy running
check.why: The install script puts the program in a folder on your search path, so the terminal finds it by name.

work: Run the install line, then check it with claude in a small project folder.
Finish sign in in the browser and run slash doctor once to see a healthy report.

title: Command not found, two copies, and surprise bills

beats.say: You installed it, typed claude, and got command not found. What went wrong?

show.sub: installed, but the terminal cannot see it

beats.say: Usually the terminal started before the install changed its search path, the list of folders it checks for programs. Open a fresh terminal window and try again. If it still fails, run slash doctor, which reports the version, how it was installed, and config problems.
Watch for two copies. If you used both the native installer and Homebrew, the terminal may run the older one. Also, the native install updates itself, while Homebrew needs a manual upgrade.

show.title: Duplicate installs
items: Native plus Homebrew means two copies
The terminal runs whichever it finds first
Native self updates, Homebrew does not

beats.say: And billing differs. A subscription hits usage limits and waits. A Console account never stops, but every token costs money, so a runaway session becomes a bill.

check.q: After install, claude says command not found. What do you try first?
opts: Reinstall with Homebrew on top
Open a fresh terminal window, then run slash doctor if it still fails
Create a new Console account
check.why: A terminal opened before the install often has a stale search path. A fresh window fixes it, and slash doctor diagnoses the rest.

work: Run which claude and confirm only one install exists.
Note how you update: automatic for native, manual upgrade for Homebrew.
If using a Console account, set a spend limit before long sessions.

title: Rolling out sign in and install across a team

beats.say: Fifty engineers need Claude Code. Do you let each person pick their own install and login?

Probably not. Personal subscriptions tie company code to private accounts, and you cannot see or cap the spend. Console accounts give central billing, usage visibility, and spend limits, at the price of paying per token.
For installs, native auto-updates keep everyone current but move versions under you. Homebrew or a pinned image gives control and repeatability, but someone must own upgrades.

show.title: Install trade-off
items: Pinning needs an owner for upgrades

beats.say: For iPad users or locked laptops, a Codespace avoids local installs entirely. You trade setup pain for hourly cloud cost and a network dependency.

check.q: Why prefer a central Console account over personal subscriptions for a company team?
opts: It is always cheaper per developer
It gives central billing, visibility and spend limits for company work
It removes the need to install anything
check.why: Control and visibility matter at team scale. Per-token billing is not always cheaper, but you can see and cap it.

work: Pick one sign-in route for work use and write it in the onboarding doc.
Decide whether to let native auto-update or pin a version, and name who owns upgrades.
Offer the Codespace for people who cannot install locally.

title: Look before you build

beats.say: Would you let a builder knock down a wall before looking at the house?
Of course not. A good builder walks through first, looks around, and touches nothing. That is exploring. Claude Code should start the same way: read, then report.
Next, the builder shows you a plan. Which walls, what it costs, how they will check it is safe. Only after you say yes do they pick up tools.

show.title: The plan
items: How we check it is safe
You say yes, then work starts

beats.say: At the end, you inspect the work yourself, then sign. The signature is your commit, a saved snapshot with a note about what changed. Your name is on it.

check.q: In the builder story, what should happen before any tools come out?
opts: The builder starts with the biggest wall
The builder looks around and shares a plan you approve
You sign the work
Nothing, the builder decides alone
check.why: Exploring and planning come first, so mistakes are caught while they are still cheap.

work: Next time you ask for a fix, start with: read these files and change nothing.
Ask for a plan before you approve any edit.

title: Explore, plan, code, commit

beats.say: Why does asking Claude to just fix the bug so often go wrong?
Because it guesses. So step one, explore. Say: read the ingest file and its test file, change nothing, tell me which tests fail and why. Reading is free. Mistakes are not.
Step two, plan mode. Ask for the smallest fix for the date window bug, the files it will touch, and how it will prove the fix works. Maybe two files and one test.

show.title: Step two: plan mode
items: Smallest fix for the date window bug
List the files it will touch
State how it will prove the fix

beats.say: Step three, approve and let it edit, then run the tests itself. Step four, read the git diff yourself, ask what could this break, and commit with a message explaining the bug.

check.q: What belongs in the explore step?
opts: Letting Claude edit and test in one go
Reading the files and diagnosing failing tests without changes
Committing the fix
Writing the commit message
check.why: Explore is read-only diagnosis so the later plan rests on facts, not guesses.

work: Write an explore prompt that ends with: do not change anything yet.
Ask every plan to name the files and the proof, such as which test.

title: Green tests that lie

beats.say: What goes wrong when the plan looks great but the tests are green for the wrong reason?
Claude can make tests pass by editing the test, loosening an assertion, or special casing the input. Green only means something if you know which files changed. So read the diff, not the summary.

chip.text: Trust the diff, not the summary

beats.say: Gotchas. Explore without a no change instruction and it may edit early. A fix to a date window can shift boundaries, so ask what could this break: time zones, midnight, empty days. Stage only the intended files.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Say change nothing, or it may edit early
Check time zones, midnight, empty days

check.q: Tests pass after Claude's fix. What is the best next move?
opts: Commit straight away
Read the diff, including test files, and ask what could break
Ask Claude if it is sure
Rerun the tests until they pass twice
check.why: Passing tests can be gamed or can miss edge cases. Only the diff shows what actually changed.

work: Check that test files in the diff changed only when you meant them to.
Add edge cases for time zones and boundaries before you accept date logic.

title: Right-sizing the workflow

beats.say: When is the four step workflow too heavy, and when is it too light?
For a typo or a rename, planning costs more than the change. Just do it and check the diff. For a migration touching forty files, one session is too small.

Scale it with risk. Large work, split into plans that each commit separately, so you can revert one piece. Add guardrails that do not rely on memory: required tests in CI, protected branches, and human review before merge. Exploration burns context, so keep it narrow.

show.title: Scale it safely
items: Split big work into small commits
Each piece can be reverted alone

check.q: A forty file migration is planned. What is the best approach?
opts: One huge plan and one commit
Skip the plan and iterate
Several small plans, each tested and committed separately
Let CI be the only review
check.why: Small committed steps keep diffs reviewable and let you revert one piece without losing the rest.

work: Define which change types skip planning, such as typos and renames.
Make CI tests and human review mandatory for merges of AI-written code.

title: Driving with a hand on the brake

beats.say: What if you could hire a very fast assistant, but keep a hand on the brake the whole time?

show.text: Fast helper. Your hand on the brake.

beats.say: Think of Claude as the driver and you as the passenger holding the map. Typing the at sign and a file name is like pointing at a building on that map. Pressing Escape is the brake. It stops, waits, and loses nothing.
Plan mode is sketching the route before you drive. Clear is starting a fresh trip, so old directions do not confuse the new one. And when it asks permission, you can simply say no and explain why.

show.title: Your everyday controls
items: Plan mode: sketch the route first
Clear: a fresh trip for a new task
Say no: it adapts when you explain why

check.q: You press Escape while Claude is in the middle of a step. What happens?
opts: Everything so far is deleted
It stops and waits, and nothing is lost
The session closes
It finishes the step anyway
check.why: Escape is a brake, not an eject. Claude pauses and waits for your next instruction, and the work done so far stays.

work: Practice pressing Escape once during a harmless task, to see it stop and wait.
Next time a permission prompt looks odd, say no and give a one-line reason.

title: The keys that steer a session

beats.say: How do you steer Claude without leaving the keyboard?

show.text: Four moves cover most of the day

beats.say: Type at, then pick a file, like explain at pipeline slash ingest dot py. Claude reads exactly that file instead of guessing. Start a line with an exclamation mark to run a shell command yourself, like python three dash m unittest dash q. The output lands in the conversation, so Claude sees the test result.
Press Escape to stop mid-step. Press it twice, or type slash rewind, to jump back to an earlier message and carry on from there.
Shift plus Tab cycles modes. Stop at plan mode to get a plan before any edit.

check.q: You want Claude to see your test results without it running them. What do you do?
opts: Type an at sign before the test name
Start the line with an exclamation mark and run the command
Press Escape twice
Use slash model
check.why: A line starting with the exclamation mark runs the shell command yourself, and its output goes into the conversation where Claude can read it.

work: Use at to point to a file in your next question instead of describing where it lives.
Run your test command with a leading exclamation mark and ask Claude to fix what fails.

title: Context, resume and permission traps

beats.say: Why does Claude seem to get worse an hour into a session?

show.text: A full context is a foggy context

beats.say: Everything you say, every file it reads, every command output sits in its context, a fixed-size working memory. As it fills, early details get crowded out. Type slash context to see what is eating the space.
Bang commands help, but a noisy test log pastes hundreds of lines into that memory. Slash clear between unrelated tasks. To resume yesterday, run claude dash c, or claude dash r to choose.

show.title: Keep it tidy
items: claude -c continues, claude -r lets you choose

beats.say: Allow always applies to that kind of command in this project, so read the prompt before you click it. Rewind rolls back the conversation, but do not assume it undoes something outside, like a database write.

show.title: Two gotchas
items: Allow always covers a kind of command, in this project
Rewind is not a promise to undo outside effects

check.q: Two unrelated tasks later, Claude keeps mixing up details from the first. Best fix?
opts: Rewind twice
Run slash clear before the new task
Switch to accept edits
Allow always
check.why: Old context from an unrelated task crowds and confuses the new one. Clearing gives a clean conversation.

work: Run slash context during a long session and note which item is largest.
Review your allow always rules for this project and remove any that are too broad.

title: When not to trust the autopilot

beats.say: When is pressing accept edits a mistake?

show.text: Accept edits trades review for speed
show.sub: Know when to pay for review

beats.say: It is safe after an approved plan, for a small change, with tests that give a fast verdict. It is risky on unfamiliar code, shared configuration, or anything touching production data. There, keep the prompts on.

Permissions control your blast radius. Allow always is scoped to this project, so a loose rule in a scratch repo is a different risk than in a deploy repo. Prefer narrow rules, and say no with a reason.

Cost matters too. Long sessions carry big context, so clear often. Use slash model to match effort: a lighter model for renames, a stronger one for design. Plan first, accept edits second, then verify with a bang test run.

check.q: Which situation best justifies staying out of accept edits mode?
opts: A renamed variable in a tested file
An approved plan for a small change
Editing shared deployment configuration you do not know well
Fixing a typo in a comment
check.why: Shared, unfamiliar configuration has a large blast radius and weak fast feedback, so per-edit review is worth its cost.

work: Write a team rule: plan mode first, accept edits only for small, tested changes.
Audit allow always rules per repo, with the strictest in deploy and production repos.
Pick a lighter model for mechanical tasks and a stronger one for design work.
